'''''Nymphaea nouchali''''', often known by its [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Nymphaea stellata''''', or by [[common name]]s '''blue lotus''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 20 April 2015}}</ref> '''star lotus''', '''red water lily''', '''dwarf aquarium lily''', '''blue water lily''', '''blue star water lily''' or '''manel flower''', is a [[Nymphaeaceae|water lily]] of genus ''[[Nymphaea]]''. It is native to southern and eastern parts of Asia, and is the [[List of national flowers|national flower]] of [[Bangladesh]]<ref name="bd"/> and [[Sri Lanka]]. This species is usually considered to include the blue Egyptian lotus [[Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea|''N. nouchali'' var. ''caerulea'']].<ref>{{citation	
|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/search?q=Nymphaea+nouchali
|title=The Plant List: A Working List of All Plant Species
|access-date=20 April 2015}}</ref> In the past, taxonomic confusion has occurred, with the name ''Nymphaea nouchali'' incorrectly applied to ''[[Nymphaea pubescens]]''.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242000584 |title=Flora of China online |access-date=20 April 2015 |author1=Dezhi Fu |author2=John H. Wiersema |author3=Donald Padgett |name-list-style=amp |volume=6}}</ref>

==Description==
''N. nouchali'' is a day-blooming non-viviparous plant with submerged roots and stems. Part of the leaves are submerged, while others rise slightly above the surface. The leaves are round and green on top; they usually have a darker underside. The floating leaves have undulating edges that give them a [[crenellate]]d appearance. Their size is about {{convert|20-23|cm|in|abbr=on}} and their spread is up to {{convert|1.5|m|ft}} from the rhizome.<ref name = "lim_nymphaea_2014">{{Cite book| publisher = Springer Netherlands| isbn = 978-94-017-8748-2| pages = 519–525| last = Lim| first = T. K.| title = Edible Medicinal and Non Medicinal Plants: Volume 8, Flowers| chapter = ''Nymphaea nouchali''| location = Dordrecht| date = 2014| doi = 10.1007/978-94-017-8748-2_37| chapter-url = https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-8748-2_37}}</ref>

This water lily has a beautiful flower which is usually white or blue in color. Its variants occur in white, blue, violet, purple, pink & cream/yellowish white colours. The flower has four or five [[sepal]]s and 13-15 [[petal]]s that have an angular appearance, making the flower look star-shaped from above. The cup-like [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] has a diameter of {{convert|4-15|cm|in|abbr=on}}.

===Cytology===
The chromosome count is n = 38 or n = 42. The genome size is 1193.16 Mb.<ref name = "Chen et al., 2017">{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/hortres.2017.51 |doi-access=free |title=Water lilies as emerging models for Darwin's abominable mystery |year=2017 |last1=Chen |first1=Fei |last2=Liu |first2=Xing |last3=Yu |first3=Cuiwei |last4=Chen |first4=Yuchu |last5=Tang |first5=Haibao |last6=Zhang |first6=Liangsheng |journal=Horticulture Research |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=17051 |pmid=28979789 |pmc=5626932 |bibcode=2017HorR....417051C }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was first described by [[Nicolaas Laurens Burman]] in [[1768]].<ref name = "POWO, 2023" /> The species concept was significantly expanded by [[Bernard Verdcourt]] in 1989. Several species, namely ''[[Nymphaea caerulea]]'' {{au|Savigny}}, ''[[Nymphaea ovalifolia]]'' {{au|Conard}}, ''[[Nymphaea colorata]]'' {{au|Peter}}, and ''[[Nymphaea petersiana]]'' {{au|Klotzsch}} were merged into ''Nymphaea nouchali'' as new varieties. Additionally, two more varieties were described: ''Nymphaea nouchali'' var. ''mutandaensis'' {{au|Verdc.}}<ref name = "Verdcourt, 1989">Verdcourt, B. (1989). [https://books.google.com/books?hl=de&lr=&id=VicIFn-2fQYC&oi=fnd&pg=PA1&dq=flora+of+tropical+east+africa+nymphaeaceae+verdcourt&ots=6Ec9s60r6x&sig=712FUvfsfP9RY-34tDp0WQjY_jE Flora of Tropical East Africa - Nymphaeceae] (1989) (Vol. 128). CRC Press.</ref> and [[Nymphaea nouchali var. versicolor|''Nymphaea nouchali'' var. ''versicolor'']] {{au|(Sims) Guruge & Yakand.}} published by [[Shashika Kumudumali Guruge]] and [[Deepthi Yakandawala]] in 2017.<ref name = "Guruge et al., 2017">Guruge, S., Yakandawala, D., & Yakandawala, K. (2017). A taxonomic synopsis of ''Nymphaea nouchali'' Burm. f. and infraspecific taxa. Journal of the National Science Foundation of Sri Lanka, 45(3).</ref> This broad circumscription of ''Nymphaea nouchali'' has been criticised as highly unnatural.<ref name = "Roestel et al., 2024" /> ''[[Nymphaea petersiana]]'' turned out to be a member of the subgenus [[Nymphaea subg. Lotos|''Nymphaea'' subg. ''Lotos'']] and is therefore unrelated to ''Nymphaea nouchali''.<ref name = "Roestel et al., 2024">{{cite journal | last1=Roestel | first1=Jessica A. | last2=Wiersema | first2=John H. | last3=Jansen | first3=Robert K. | last4=Borsch | first4=Thomas | last5=Gruenstaeudl | first5=Michael | title=On the importance of sequence alignment inspections in plastid phylogenomics – an example from revisiting the relationships of the water-lilies | journal=Cladistics | date=2024 | volume=40 | issue=5 | pages=469–495 | doi=10.1111/cla.12584 | pmid=38761095 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/cla.12584 }}</ref><ref name = "Borsch et al., 2007">Borsch, T., Hilu, K. W., Wiersema, J. H., Löhne, C., Barthlott, W., & Wilde, V. (2007). [https://www.seerosenforum.de/Gattung/PHYLOGENY-OF-NYMPHAEA.pdf Phylogeny of ''Nymphaea'' (Nymphaeaceae): evidence from substitutions and microstructural changes in the chloroplast trnT-trnF region.] International Journal of Plant Sciences, 168(5), 639-671.</ref><ref name = "Dkhar et al., 2010">Dkhar, J., Kumaria, S., Rao, S. R., & Tandon, P. (2010). [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304377010000458 Molecular phylogenetics and taxonomic reassessment of four Indian representatives of the genus ''Nymphaea''.] Aquatic Botany, 93(2), 135-139.</ref>
''Nymphaea nouchali'' is placed in the subgenus [[Nymphaea subg. Brachyceras|''Nymphaea'' subg. ''Brachyceras'']].<ref name = "GRIN" />

===Natural hybridisation===
[[File:Detail of Nymphaea × daubenyana W.T.Baxter ex Daubeny flower.jpg|thumb|right|Detail of ''Nymphaea'' × ''daubenyana'' flower, a natural hybrid of ''Nymphaea nouchali'' var. ''caerulea'' and ''Nymphaea micrantha''<ref name = "POWO N. × daubenyana" />]]
Together with ''[[Nymphaea micrantha]]'', ''Nymphaea nouchali'' var. ''caerulea'' forms the natural hybrid [[Nymphaea × daubenyana|''Nymphaea'' × ''daubenyana'']] native to Chad.<ref name = "POWO N. × daubenyana">{{cite POWO |id=928088-1 |title=''Nymphaea'' × ''daubenyana'' W.T.Baxter ex Daubeny |accessdate=3 July 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This aquatic plant is native in a broad region from [[Afghanistan]], the [[Indian subcontinent]], to [[Taiwan]], southeast Asia and Australia.<ref name = "POWO, 2023">{{cite POWO |id=605643-1 |title=''Nymphaea nouchali'' Burm.f. |accessdate=28 June 2023}}</ref><ref name=GRIN/> It has been long valued as a garden flower in [[Thailand]] and [[Myanmar]] to decorate ponds and gardens. In its natural state, ''N. nouchali'' is found in static or slow-flowing aquatic habitats of low to moderate depth.{{citation needed|date=June 2013}}

==Ecology==
The leaves of the lily can be affected by a water-born fungi, ''[[Doassansiopsis nymphaea]]''.<ref>Dr.V.R. Patil {{google books|cPpDCwAAQBAJ|Research on Fresh water fungi (2015)|page=113}}</ref>

==Use==
===Symbolism===
''Nymphaea nouchali'' is the national flower of [[Bangladesh]].<ref name="bd">{{cite web |url=http://www.supremecourt.gov.bd/scweb/constitution/pdf/04_part1-4.pdf |title=Constitution Of The People's Republic Of Bangladesh |publisher=[[Supreme Court of Bangladesh]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130922151255/http://supremecourt.gov.bd/scweb/constitution/pdf/04_part1-4.pdf |archive-date=2013-09-22}}</ref> A pale blue-flowered ''N. nouchali'' is the [[national flower]] of [[Sri Lanka]], where it is known as ''nil mānel'' or ''nil mahanel'' ({{lang|si|නිල් මානෙල්}}).<ref name="slanka2">{{cite news|url=http://www.sundaytimes.lk/101107/Plus/plus_01.html|title=The Great Pretender|last=Hettiarachchi|first=Kumudini|date=November 7, 2010|work=The Sunday Times, Sri Lanka|access-date=24 June 2013}}</ref>

In [[Sri Lanka]], this plant usually grows in [[water buffalo|buffalo]] ponds and natural [[wetlands]].
Its beautiful aquatic flower has been mentioned in [[Sanskrit]], [[Pali]], and [[Sinhala language|Sinhala]] literary works since ancient times under the names ''kuvalaya'', ''kumuda'', ''indhīwara'', ''niluppala'', ''nilōtpaḷa'', and ''nilupul'' as a symbol of virtue, discipline, and purity. [[Buddhist]] lore in Sri Lanka claims that this flower was one of the 108 auspicious signs found on Prince [[Gautama Buddha|Siddhartha]]'s footprint.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://park.org/Japan/TokyoNet/aip/search/all/stats.html|title=National Stats of Bangladesh|website=park.org}}</ref> It is said that when Buddha died, lotus flowers blossomed everywhere he had walked in his lifetime.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

[[Claire Waight Keller]] included the plant to represent Bangladesh and Sri Lanka in [[Meghan Markle]]'s [[Wedding dress of Meghan Markle#Veil|wedding veil]], which included the distinctive flora of each [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] country.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.royal.uk/wedding-dress-bridesmaids%E2%80%99-dresses-and-page-boys-uniforms|title=The Wedding Dress, Bridesmaids' Dresses and Page Boys' Uniforms|last=Jenny.minard|date=19 May 2018|website=The Royal Family}}</ref>

''N. nouchali'' might have been one of the plants eaten by the [[Lotophagi]] of [[Homer]]'s ''[[Odyssey]]''.{{citation needed|date=November 2016}}

===Horticulture===
    {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2025}}
''N. nouchali'' is used as an ornamental plant because of its spectacular flowers, and is most commonly used for the traditional and cultural festivals in Sri Lanka. It is also popular as an aquarium plant under the name "dwarf lily" or "dwarf red lily".<ref>{{Cite web |title=How to Care for a Dwarf Aquarium Lily (Nymphaea stellata) |url=https://www.aquariumcoop.com/blogs/aquarium/dwarf-aquarium-lily-care |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=Aquarium Co-Op |language=en}}</ref> Sometimes, it is grown for its flowers, while other aquarists prefer to trim the lily pads, and just have the underwater foliage.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

===Herbal medicine===
    {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2025}}
''N. nouchali'' is considered a medicinal plant in Indian [[Ayurvedic]] medicine under the name ''ambal''; it was mainly used to treat indigestion.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

===Food===
Like all water lilies, its pear-shaped, brown cottony-covered, potato-sized [[rhizome]]s, leaves and most of the plant are poisonous, and contain an [[alkaloid]] called [[nupharin]]. Unlike European species, this can (and must) be neutralised in the rhizomes of this species by boiling. In India these have been eaten as a [[famine food]] or as a medicinal. In [[Vietnam]] it was eaten roasted. In [[Sri Lanka]] it was formerly eaten as a type of medicine and its price was too high to serve as a normal meal, but in the 1940s some villagers began to cultivate the water lilies in the [[paddy field]]s left uncultivated during the [[monsoon]] season (Yala season), and the price dropped. It is eaten boiled and in curries. The [[tuber]]s of this species are completely edible, during the [[dry season]] they consist almost entirely of starch, and were eaten in [[West Africa]], usually boiled or roasted.<ref>{{cite journal | jstor=4115519 | title=Waterlilies as Food | last1=Irvine | first1=F. R. |author-link=Frederick Robert Irvine |last2=Trickett | first2=R. S. | journal=Kew Bulletin | year=1953 | volume=8 | issue=3 | pages=363–370 | doi=10.2307/4115519 | bibcode=1953KewBu...8..363I }}</ref>

In Bangladesh, the stems of ''Nymphaea nouchali'', known locally as shapla, are widely consumed as a vegetable. The dish, commonly called shaplar data, is cooked with mustard seeds, spices, and sometimes dried fish. Unlike some regions where the plant is used as a famine food, it is a regular part of rural diets and seasonal cuisine in Bangladesh.{{citation needed|date=July 2025}}

The dried plant is collected from ponds, tanks, and marshes during the dry season and used in India as animal [[forage]].<ref>{{cite journal |first1=A. |last1=Banerjee |first2=S |last2=Matai |year=1990 |title=Composition of Indian aquatic plants in relation to utilization as animal forage |url=https://www.apms.org/wp-content/uploads/japm-28-02-069.pdf |journal=Journal of Aquatic Plant Management |volume=28 |pages=69–73}}</ref>
